summary: Describes the framework for the RFC Series and the RFC Editor function, built on organized community involvement and accountability as the Internet technical community grew. It obsoletes RFC 4844.

eli5.summary: The RFC series is a long library of internet documents. This describes how the library is run so it keeps serving the community.

questions: what does the rfc editor do
subtitle: The IAB's framework for who runs the RFC Series, who approves documents, and how the four streams fit together.

tldr.problem: As the Internet community grew, it was unclear where community involvement ended and RFC Editor control began, and how series-wide issues should be settled fairly across all sources of RFCs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC Editor handles day-to-day operation, the IAB oversees policy and verifies community input, the IETF LLC and IASA fund and contract the work, and four streams each approve their own documents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8729 replaces RFC 4844, updating it for the IASA restructuring and the IETF LLC.

today: RFC 8729 is an Informational RFC published in February 2020 that obsoletes RFC 4844. It has been updated by RFC 9280 and RFC 9920.

sections.title: Why a Framework
sections.content:
The first RFC was published in April 1969. The RFC Series is the archival series dedicated to documenting Internet technical specifications, covering both general contributions from the research and engineering community and standards documents. IETF documents are a large part, but not the entirety, of the series.

Past confusion over where to address issues specific to contributing groups (the IETF, the IAB or independent individuals) sometimes caused tension. Without an agreed framework, discussions risked becoming polarized: either the IETF dictating to the rest of the series, or the series imposing undue restrictions on the IETF. The IAB, which has a responsibility for the RFC Editor in its charter, provides this framework to settle that.
sections.eli5: When many different groups share one library, they need clear rules about who decides what. This document writes those rules down.

sections.title: The RFC Series Mission
sections.content: The mission is a single statement: the RFC Series is the archival series dedicated to documenting Internet technical specifications, including general contributions from the Internet research and engineering community as well as standards documents. RFCs are available free of charge to anyone via the Internet.
sections.eli5: The library keeps a permanent copy of important internet papers, and anyone can read them for free.

sections.title: Roles and Responsibilities
sections.content:
The RFC Editor started as one person and now means a collection of experts and organizations. It is the expert technical and series editor, implementing the editorial management of the series and leading discussion of policy for editing, publishing and archiving.

The IAB ensures the mission is fulfilled for the whole community. It lacks comprehensive publishing expertise, so it focuses on principles and on informing and consulting the right bodies. It approves the appointment of the RFC Editor and the general policy the RFC Editor follows, and it monitors how well policies are working.

For operations, the IETF LLC (part of the IASA) is responsible for administrative and financial matters, and the IASA funds the RFC Editor. The IETF Executive Director provides contractual and financial oversight and works with the IAB to find the RFC Production Center and RFC Publisher (roles defined in RFC 8728). The RFC Series Oversight Committee, acting with authority delegated from the IAB, makes sure the series is run in a transparent and accountable manner.
sections.eli5: One group does the daily work, one group makes sure the rules are fair, and one group pays the bills and signs the contracts.

sections.title: The Four-Part Framework
sections.content:
The framework supports the operational implementation of the series, based on public process and definition documents, with clear responsibilities and mechanisms for change. It covers four categories of activity: approval of documents; editing, processing and publication; archiving, indexing and accessibility; and series-wide rules and guidelines.

For each category the pattern is the same. The RFC Editor handles operations. When a process needs to change, the IAB works with the RFC Editor and other parties to get community input and verifies that the change accounts for community requirements. Archiving has no community process document; the text says the archive continues as built by the RFC Editors since the series began. Series-wide rules include the RFC Style Guide (RFC 7322) and the copyright rules in RFC 5378.
sections.eli5: For every job in the library, there is a person who does it, and a way to change the rules if people want something different.

sections.title: The Four RFC Streams
sections.content:
Contributions arrive through streams, each with its own approval process. The text expects no new streams and prefers that none be created.

  • IETF stream: working group documents and individual submissions sponsored by an area director. It is the only stream that can approve Standards Track or BCP RFCs, following the process in RFC 2026.
  • IAB stream: approved under the IAB's own process, described in RFC 4845.
  • IRTF stream: the IRTF is chartered as an activity of the IAB and, with IAB approval, defines its own non-Standards-Track process, described in RFC 5743.
  • Independent Submission stream: for documents outside the other streams. Approval falls generally to the RFC Editor, who seeks input from the IESG. The model for the Independent Submission Editor is in RFC 8730.

Each stream also outlines its technical publication requirements. The IAB must agree those are consistent with, and implementable by, the RFC Editor activity, and other streams should deviate minimally from the requirements in RFC 4714.
sections.eli5: There are four doors into the library, and each door has its own guard who decides which papers may enter.

sections.title: Security and Changes Since RFC 4844
sections.content:
Publication processes must prevent unapproved changes. Because the RFC Editor maintains the index, enough security must be in place to stop outside parties changing published documents. The archive, any source documents needed to recreate RFCs, and associated originals such as errata lists and tools must be protected against failure of the storage medium and similar disasters.

Compared with RFC 4844, Sections 3.3, 3.4 and 4 were updated to match the restructured IASA, where the IETF LLC now performs tasks previously assigned to the IETF Administrative Director and the Internet Society. Many references were updated, and the wording changed from a revised framework to the framework.
sections.eli5: The library must keep its books safe from tampering and from floods and fires, and this version updated the rules for who pays and signs for it.
